SAR Domain for Semantic Segmentation
Xinyang Pu①, Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Hecheng Jia①, Member, IEEE,
Linghao Zheng, Graduate Student Member, IEEE, Feng Wang ①, Member, IEEE,
and Feng Xu, Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract—In the realm of artificial intelligence, the emergence
of foundation models, backed by high computing capabilities and
extensive data, has been revolutionary. A segment anything model
(SAM), built on the vision transformer (ViT) model with millions
of parameters and trained on its corresponding large-scale dataset
SA-1B, excels in various segmentation scenarios relying on its
significance of semantic information and generalization ability.
Such achievement of visual foundation model stimulates contin-
uous researches on specific downstream tasks in computer vision.
The classwise-SAM-adapter (CWSAM) is designed to adapt the
high-performing SAM for landcover classification on space-borne
synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images. The proposed CWSAM
freezes most of SAM's parameters and incorporates lightweight
adapters for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and a classwise mask
decoder is designed to achieve semantic segmentation task. This
adapt-tuning method allows for efficient landcover classification of
SAR images, balancing the accuracy with computational demand.
In addition, the task-specific input module injects low-frequency
information of SAR images by MLP-based layers to improve
the model performance. Compared to conventional state-of-the-
art semantic segmentation algorithms by extensive experiments,
CWSAM showcases enhanced performance with fewer computing
resources, highlighting the potential of leveraging foundational
models such as SAM for specific downstream tasks in the SAR
domain.

parameter-efficient fine-tuning, segment anything (SA), synthetic
aperture radar (SAR), visual foundation model.

images with predicted masks. (b) SAR images with predicted masks
1) SAM is hardly able to segment the SAR images for reason-
able accuracy even though it has good generalization ca-
pability on natural images including optical aerial images
as shown in Fig. 1(a). Considering the electromagnetic
wave imaging mechanism of signal echo on SAR, the
appearances of SAR images are very different with natural
scene images. To be specific, SAR images exhibit coherent
speckle noise due to wave physics, side lobes, and the
complex scattering characteristics that can introduce false
alarms, and layover and shadowing effects in regions with
steep terrain or tall structures. Specific situations of SAR
images including multiple polarization properties and low
SNR imaging circumstances are rarely involved in SAM.
2) The category-agnostic property of SAM hinders its appli-
cation on diverse visual downstream tasks. For semantic
segmentation and landcover classification tasks on SAR
images, each pixel needs a predicted category while SAM
only generates several binary mask lack of classwise infor-
mation under the guidance of prompt input. The segment
results of SAR images from SAM represent almost no
meaningful semantic information as shown in Fig. 1(b)
because pixels in the same category are not classified into
the same category. In addition, landcover classification
task demand the model to output a multiclass predicted
mask for each image while the quantity of output masks
by SAM is variable.
Therefore, we propose a method named classwise-SAM-
adapter (CWSAM) to achieve reasonable performance on pixel-
level SAR landcover classification task by leveraging founda-
tion model SAM and adding a classwise light-weighted mask
decoder. A well-designed adapter fine-tuning mechanism is uti-
lized. Freezing most parameters of the heavy vision transformer
(ViT) [8] image encoder of SAM and inserting a small number
of trainable parameters by adapters, CWSAM shifts the natural
scene domain of SAM to SAR domain, and explores the poten-
tial application of large model in SAR downstream tasks such
as landcover classification. Since only limited parameters are
trainable with gradient in the model weight, CWSAM demands
low computing resources and makes training process efficient.
We construct CWSAM as a preliminary attempt of visual
foundation model application in SAR images and believe that
such effective methods with viable computing cost will bring
good future on the development of foundation model to SAR
intelligent interpretation. Extensive experiments illustrate that
the efficiency and reliability of the proposed method on both
segmentation performance and training process. CWSAM out-
performs multiple state-of-the-art semantic segmentation al-
gorithms with fewer trainable parameters and less memory
consumption. To our best knowledge, it is the first time that
SAM is introduced for parameter-efficient fine-tuning on SAR
domain to realize semantic segmentation downstream task with
category-aware ability.
In summary, the contributions of this article can be summa-
rized as follows.
1) The proposed CWSAM introduces an end-to-end archi-
tecture with light-weighted adapters inserted in the image
encoder of SAM for efficient parameter fine-tuning on
large models. The method transfers the natural scene do-
main of SAM to the SAR domain. By leveraging the visual
foundation model, it achieves a reliable performance on
landcover classification tasks using SAR images.
2) A classwise mask decoder of CWSAM is designed to
expand classwise attribute to original category-agnostic
SAM model for fine-grained semantic segmentation
downstream task. For SAR images, the light-weight class-
wise upscaling convolution layer in the classwise mask de-
coder is utilized to identify multiple landcover categories
on pixel level.
3) The task-specific input module of SAR image low-
frequency information is conducted to provide sufficient
semantic information of landcover characteristics through
2-D image fast Fourier transform in the end-to-end archi-
tecture automatically for enhancing segmentation perfor-
mance.
Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that CWSAM sur-
passes multiple existing semantic segmentation algorithms with-
out the high requirements of computing costs. Even though
meeting the characteristic difference between SAR and natural
images of SAM, the proposed method achieves to employ the
advantages of foundation model to improve the segmentation
performance on SAR images.

II. RELATED WORKS
A. Segment Anything Model
SAM is released by Meta AI Research in the segment anything
(SA) project for image segmentation and shows impressive
zero-shot performance and powerful generalization on multi-
ple application scenes [9]. SAM conducts a ViT-based image
encoder, a light-weighted mask decoder, and a flexible prompt
encoder allowing inputs of points, bounding boxes, masks, and
texts. Inspired by the booming large language model (LLM) in
NLP, the image encoder of SAM adopts the basic architecture of
ViT and has three different sizes of models, including ViT-Base,
ViT-Huge, and ViT-Large. MAE [10] method is explored to
pretrain the ViT that can process high resolution input images.
SAM has powerful zero-shot abilities by prompt engineering
that contains two types of prompts: sparse prompt (points, boxes,
and text) and dense prompt (mask). Positional encoding [11]
is responsible for extracting prompt embeddings of points and
boxes, and CLIP [12] is responsible for text prompts. Dense
prompts are embedded by the convolution module and summed
elementwise to fuse with image embedding. Multiple prompt
methods enable the users to concentrate on various scenes and
objects, and bring strong application flexibility relying on SAM
zero-shot advantages. In addition, the mask decoder provides
three output masks of diverse scopes for per image input to
address the issue of ambiguous prompt.
B. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of SAM
Leveraging the data engine and SA-1B dataset with billions of
masks, SAM is regarded as a foundation model of segmentation
in computer vision and simulates diverse exploration algorithms
on utilizing SAM for downstream tasks on various application
fields. The authors in [13], [14], and [15] explore the potential
of SAM on medical image analysis, the authors in [16] and [17]
focus on camouflaged object detection, and Ahmadi et al. [18]
focus on infrastructure detection. Mirror and transparent objects
detection task based on SAM is also involved in [19].
Furthermore, for aerial images, several researches [20], [21]
robe the generalization of SAM under typical gap between
natural scenes of SAM and remote sensing. Wang et al. [22]
develop SAM as an efficient annotation system to produce the
large-scale remote sensing segmentation dataset called SAMRS.
The authors in [23] and [24] conduct prompt engineering to opti-
mize SAM for downstream segmentation task on remote sensing
images. RingMo [25]leverages generative self-supervised learn-
ing to build a foundation model for remote sensing, and then, it
is combined with SAM to achieve a foundation model for mul-
timodal remote-sensing image segmentation called RingMo-
SAM [26]. SCD-SAM [27] combines MobileSAM and CNN
to extract progressive semantic change features for remote sens-
ing images through adapter-based PEFT technology. Osco [28]
explores the potential of SAM for remote sensing applications
including zero shot and one shot problems. RSAM-Seg [29]
integrates prior knowledge into SAM and utilizes adapter fine-
tuning for remote sensing image semantic segmentation. Road-
SAM [30] leverages SAM's powerful generalization for high
resolution road extraction in optical remote sensing images.
Considering full fine-tuning a large model is difficult due to
the high demand of computing resources and available data,
most of these SAM fine-tuning researches follow the main-
stream parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods of transformer
architecture inspired by LLMs and NLP technologies, including
adding additional parameters, selecting a part of parameters
to update, and introducing reparametrization. The methods of
adding additional parameters can be roughly divided into two
types: inserting extra adapter modules [31] and soft prompts
fine-tuning [32], [33].
C. Semantic Segmentation and SAR Landcover Classification
Semantic segmentation plays an essential role on computer vi-
sion and has made great achievements on proposing a variety of
deep learning-based algorithms. Regarded as an extension task
from image classification to pixel-level image segmentation,
semantic segmentation starts from a fundamental architecture
of fully convolutional networks named FCN [34] and emerges
manifold model designs and different structures of mask de-
coders to improve the segmentation performance. Subsequently,
various encoder-decoder architectures [35], [36] are optimized
with attention mechanisms [37], [38], proper receptive filed [39],
[40], high-resolution feature pyramid [41], [42], dilated convo-
lutions [43], [44], and so on. Transformer-based algorithms [45],
[46] conduct great performance on semantic segmentation task.
The requirements of pixel-level semantic segmentation ap-
plications on SAR images tend to be urgent with the develop-
ment of high-resolution SAR technologies [47], [48]. Several
modified FCNs network are proposed for wetland semantic
segmentation task on SAR images [49] and PolSAR image
semantic segmentation task [50] through transfer learning. The
authors in [51], [52], and [53] utilize the FCNs networks as
baseline and focus on the single category on segmentation tasks
of SAR images, such as oil spill, road, and building. The authors
in [54] and [55] explored the landcover semantic segmentation
tasks containing multiple categories on GF-3 SAR images via
an encoder-decoder structure and a transformer architecture.
MCANet [56] proposed a multimodal-cross-attention network
to achieve land use classification task by fusing the feature
map of both optical and SAR images, as well as CFNet [57].
SCNN [58] utilizes the statistical convolutional neural network
to encode and analyze the statistical properties of the SAR image
for landcover classification on the TerraSAR-X data.

A. Adapted ViT-Based Image Encoder
The image encoder of SAM is pretrained on the SA-1B dataset
and containing rich semantic information of extensive natural
scenes in the real world, so its well iterated parameters are
beneficial for downstream task adaption. Therefore, as shown
in the ViT image encoder at the left part of Fig. 2, in order
to leverage SAM as a fundamental backbone, we maintain
the original architecture of SAM's image encoder unchanged,

B. Classwise Mask Decoder and Loss Function
To represent the multiple categories of every pixels, a class-
wise mask decoder is built on the original architecture of the
mask decoder in SAM [1] and consists of a category pre-
diction head to achieve landcover classification task. In the
classwise mask decoder of the proposed CWSAM algorithm,
the dynamic mask prediction head is ignored so that only one
mask result is obtained and involved for computing the training
losses.
1) Architecture: The framework of the classwise mask en-
coder is explained in Fig. 4. At the beginning, two two-way trans-
former blocks are explored to extract features of all embeddings,
including image embedding and prompt embedding. Multiple
attention mechanisms are employed, such as self-attention for
prompt embedding and cross-attention between image embed-
ding and prompt embedding with two directions (image-to-
prompt embedding and prompt-to-image embedding). An up-
scaling convolution block of the SAM mask decoder prepares
the final output binary mask.
However, with binary mask results, the original design of the
mask decoder of SAM is unable to figure out classification
on pixel level for semantic segmentation task. Therefore, a
classwise light-weighted convolution module named classwise
upscaling convolution is implemented for multiclasses mask
prediction by outputting the channel dimension corresponding
to the number of categories to generate classwise segmentation
masks. After the upscaling output convolution block of the SAM
mask decoder, the classwise upscaling convolution module is
added with all randomly initialized parameters trained from
scratch to finish final multiclasses mask prediction. The up-
scale convolution module composes of a deconvolutional layer,
a ReLU activation layer, and a convolution block to enlarge
semantic feature to generate final mask prediction of N classes
channels for separate category.

IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
A. Experimental Dataset and Settings
Two landcover classification datasets of SAR images are
utilized for evaluation experiments of the proposed method,
FUSAR-Map1.0 [54] and FUSAR-Map2.0 [55]. Both datasets
contain multiple categories of landcover annotations, and rep-
resent rich semantic information for SAR image interpretation,
while FUSAR-Map2.0 raises higher requirements to algorithms
by extreme data distribution and detailed label. All input SAR
images were copied from a single channel into three three-
channel images of the same value to fit the SAM pretrained
model structure. The preprocessing of the SAR images has
been completed by the publishers of FUSAR-Map1.0 and can
be directly accessed through open-source website, including
pixel-level quantization and the pixel mean contrast-stretching
method [61]. Simple normalization is involved in Pytorch at the
initialization of dataset loading and no data augmentation strate-
gies are conducted in the experiments for intuitive comparison
of algorithm performance.
1) FUSAR-Map1.0: The FUSAR-Map1.0 dataset comprises
610 GF-3 satellite SAR images of size 1024 × 1024 pixels
from 12 scenes of six provinces in China. The annotations
contain four landcover categories, building, vegetation,
water, and road. One scene of Wuhan city is selected
for test dataset and cut into 80 slices. The other eleven
senses generate total 530 SAR images of size 1024 ×
1024 for training dataset. In addition, parts of pixels
in images do not have category labels because of their
illegible appearances and are excluded from both training
and evaluation processes.

fine-grained semantic information of landcover cate-

category is extremely unbalance, which brings challenges
to segmentation models. Total ten scenes from various
countries are included in this dataset, the proportion of
training and testing scenes is 8:2. Cropped to the slides
of size 1024 × 1024 pixels, the FUSAR-Map2.0 consists
of total 738 image samples, and 549 for training and 189
for testing. The annotation distribution of every category

Feng Wang (Member, IEEE) received the B.S. and
M.S. degrees in remote sensing from Information
Engineering University, Zhengzhou, China, in 2006
and 2010, respectively, and the Ph.D. degree from in
electronic engineering Fudan University, Shanghai,
China, in 2017.
He was a Visiting Scholar with the Technical Uni-
versity of Munich, Munich, Germany, in 2013, and
a Postdoctoral Research Fellow with the State Key
Laboratory of Lunar and Planetary Sciences, Macau
University of Science and Technology, Macau, China,

Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai, as an Assistant Research Fellow. He
is currently an Associate Professor with the Key Laboratory for Information
Science of Electromagnetic Waves (Ministry of Education), School of Informa-
tion Science and Technology, Fudan University. His research interests include
SAR/ISAR Imaging, target recognition, and UAV borne remote sensing.
Feng Xu (Senior Member, IEEE) received the B.E.
degree (Hons.) in information engineering from
Southeast University, Nanjing, China, in 2003, and
the Ph.D. degree (Hons.) in electronic engineering
from Fudan University, Shanghai, China, in 2008.
From 2008 to 2010, he was a Postdoctoral Fellow
with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Adminis-
tration (NOAA) Center for Satellite Applications and
Research, Camp Springs, MD, USA. From 2010 to
2013, he worked with Intelligent Automation Inc.,
Rockville, MD, USA, and NASA Goddard Space
Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA, as a Research Scientist. In 2012, he was
selected for China's Global Experts Recruitment Program, and subsequently,
returned to Fudan University, in 2013, where he is currently a Professor and the
Vice Dean with the School of Information Science and Technology and the Vice
Director with the Key Laboratory for Information Science of Electromagnetic
Waves (MoE). His research interests include electromagnetic scattering model-
ing, SAR information retrieval, and radar system development.
Dr. Xu was the recipient of the second-class National Nature Science Award
of China in 2011, the 2014 Early Career Award of the IEEE Geoscience and
Remote Sensing Society (GRSS), and the 2007 SUMMA Graduate Fellowship
in the advanced electromagnetics area. He is a Topic Associate Editor for IEEE
TRANSACTIONS ON GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING and was an AsSOciate
Editor of IEEE GEOSCIENCE AND REMOTE SENSING LETTERS (2014–2021). He
is the Founding Chair of the IEEE GRSS Shanghai Chapter and an IEEE GRSS
AdCom Member.
